tagline: A garden, an artist’s memorial and islands shaped by changing access.
intro: Airlie Road appears among the coastal-plain routes in North Carolina’s scenic-byway guide. In Wilmington, Airlie Gardens preserves a public garden of 67 acres; east of the city, Wrightsville Beach includes a beach island and the interior Harbor Island.

Access to this coast changed in stages. Shell Road connected Wilmington to the edge of the present Intracoastal Waterway in 1887. The 1926 causeway reached Harbor Island; a highway and car bridge brought road access to the beach in 1935. At Airlie, a different change came in 1999, when New Hanover County purchased the gardens.

Begin with Airlie Gardens and the Bottle Chapel honoring artist Minnie Evans, then continue toward Wrightsville Beach. The water crossings explain the island geography: the Intracoastal Waterway separates Harbor Island from the mainland, and Banks Channel separates it from the beach.

moments.title: Airlie Gardens
moments.text: The Airlie Oak gives this garden a living landmark. North Carolina Forest Service employees measured the southern live oak in 2007, recording a trunk circumference exceeding 21 feet and a crown spread of 104 feet. At that time it was designated North Carolina’s largest live oak. Airlie’s name came from the Jones family’s home in Scotland; New Hanover County purchased the gardens in 1999. Artist Minnie Evans, who worked at the admissions gate, painted the oak in 1954. That painting is displayed at the Smithsonian American Art Museum. Mount Lebanon Chapel and its cemetery also occupy the garden grounds.

moments.title: Minnie Evans Bottle Chapel
moments.text: Reused glass bottles form a memorial to Minnie Evans inside Airlie Gardens. Evans became the gardens’ gatekeeper in 1948 and retired in 1974. She hung her artwork on the front gate to sell it, and the gardens supplied inspiration for her nature scenes. After Evans died, Virginia Wright-Frierson designed and built the chapel, incorporating work by other artists. Along the path, children’s art inspired by Evans became 95 stepping stones, one for each year of her life. The chapel’s stained glass includes faces and figures resembling those Evans used in her own work.
moments.notice: The memorial chapel is made almost entirely from reused glass bottles.

moments.title: Wrightsville Beach
moments.text: In the eighteenth century, reaching Wrightsville Beach meant changing from land travel to a boat. A footbridge reached Harbor Island from the mainland, but the beach itself remained beyond that land connection during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Ocean View Railroad laid track across Banks Channel in 1889 to carry visitors to the oceanfront. Road connections arrived later: a causeway to Harbor Island in 1926 and a highway and car bridge to the beach in 1935. The town includes both Harbor Island and a 4.6-mile beach island, separated by Banks Channel.
